grades.quote: Priority inheritance is a simple idea: any thread that is waiting for a mutex temporarily “lends” its priority to the thread that holds the mutex. A thread that holds mutexes runs with the highest priority among its own priority and those priorities it has been lent by threads waiting for the mutexes. In the example with three threads, priority inheritance will allow the low-priority thread that holds the mutex to run as though it were highpriority until it unlocks the mutex.
grades.reason: Directly explains the lock-holder dependency underlying priority inversion and how priority inheritance resolves it.

grades.quote: The reason for this is simple: the scheduler can choose only among the runnable threads, but with the convoy phenomenon, there will only be one runnable thread; all the others will be queued up for the mutex.
grades.reason: Explains how mutex waiting overrides scheduling priorities, but focuses on convoys rather than low-priority lock-holder inversion.

grades.quote: To create a mutex with priority inheritance turned on or off, you need to pass a pointer to a mutex attribute object into `pthread_mutex_init` .
grades.reason: Provides implementation guidance for priority inheritance without explaining why a low-priority lock holder delays a high-priority thread.
Discusses priority-changing security vulnerabilities and races, not blocking through a lock or priority inversion.
